hypothesis: Can release sparks and either damage rings or fighter reactions make magical buildup and consequences clearer without losing the impact the owner liked?

evidenceInspected.method: Direct view_image inspection of 16 composite stills, each displaying A/B/C; no continuous playback.

observations.facts: At 9.3 and 11.2, B has a dark ground ring by red; C places a bright star and pale flash at red. At 11.5, C makes blue pale while B keeps blue blue and places the ring beneath. Logs record fireball damage to red at 9.25/11.1833 and melee damage to blue at 11.4333.
observations.interpretation: C makes the person receiving the consequence the strongest local feature. That is more satisfying to this lens than reading an extra floor symbol, but exact animation force remains untested.

observations.facts: At 9.6 red and blue remain colored in all alternatives; no damage flash is visible. At 12.2 B/C show a broad warm melee sweep where A has a much fainter pale shape. Log places missed red release at9.6333 and the final damaging release at12.1833; final damage/death is12.2167.
observations.interpretation: The revised melee has a recognizable sweeping form, helping sell a committed attack separately from damage. A release frame alone still does not reveal whether the swing succeeds.

observations.facts: At7.0 the falling shard has dark edges in B/C and a faint pale silhouette in A. B/C also show a broad warm sweep around red. At7.6 C makes red pale with a bright star; B keeps red colored over a dark ground ring. At8.1 all living fighter colors are intact. Logs put green death6.9833, ice impact7.2333 without damage, then yellow spread damage to red7.5667 and7.6.
observations.interpretation: B/C improve the distinct shard/sweep silhouettes. C offers the clearest sampled consequence when red runs into the spread, but does not identify yellow as the source of each incoming shot. The non-damaging shard remains important contrary evidence: a dramatic spell landing must not itself count as a hit.

observations.facts: At.2 blue/yellow have dark ground preparation marks in A and fainter pale marks in B/C. At1.0 C makes red pale while B retains red with a dark ring beneath. At1.3 a row of warm projectiles remains visible between yellow and blue across all panels; B/C have a darker ice projectile edge near red. At2.2 C makes green pale while B has a ring beneath; the falling ice has dark outline in both revisions.
observations.interpretation: The revision retains the visible rapid-fire chain rather than burying it. C momentarily costs color identity in both early exchanges; with several hits this could turn readability into flashing noise. Softer start is plausible from still samples but its smoothness and shot rhythm cannot be established.

rankedConcerns.concern: C briefly replaces the victim color with a pale flash; with small adjacent fighters, identity is weaker at exactly the consequential moment. B is safer for color tracking.

Release and damage sparks are warm and generic even around ice damage. The more visible ice shard improves elemental identity, but effects do not yet make every fighter feel like a distinctive magician.
B ground rings remain small visual instrumentation against the grid floor; the spell world feels less bodily than C. A persistent ring can be noticed without the viewer knowing who caused it.
Anticipation, preparation easing, rapid-fire timing and distraction need actual playback. Do not describe still review as approval of those qualities.

tentativePreference.label: C · Fighter flash · impact sparks
tentativePreference.confidence: low to moderate, sampled stills only
tentativePreference.reason: The hurt body carries the consequence, giving the two fireballs and melee a more direct payoff. Prefer C narrowly for magical fight spectacle; B remains a credible alternative if preserving fighter color matters more.

limitations: No continuous footage or browser playback inspected; no claims about felt rhythm, smoothness, animation force or prolonged distraction.
No calibrated owner taste model; the owner has not accepted either revision.
Three curated setups do not establish general readability across seeds or rotations.
Logs describe spell families without unique projectile lineage.
The same combat across variants supports presentation comparison only; no new tactical identity, surprising ability behavior or balance improvement follows.

displaySummary.title: C gives hits a more direct payoff
displaySummary.text: I narrowly favor the fighter flash: fireballs and melee visibly affect the person being hit. B preserves fighter colors better. The darker ice and clearer sweep help both revisions, but the generic sparks add little magical identity. This is a still-frame judgment; rhythm and distraction need playback.
